notes: Asylum appeal allowed narrowly; adjudicator's failure to address torture evidence was an error of law.

enrichment.short_title: El Rifai: asylum appeal allowed for failure to address torture risk on return
key_facts: Palestinian appellant claimed asylum after leaving Lebanon, alleging persecution linked to a 1998 Fateh-related incident and Hezbollah pressure.
The adjudicator found the 1998 incident involved a criminal enterprise and rejected Refugee Convention and Article 3 claims; the IAT dismissed a point-of-law appeal.
Country reports recorded torture and abuse by Lebanese security forces during preliminary investigations.
The adjudicator considered prison conditions but did not address the torture evidence in his reasons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision on a point of law under section 101(1) of the 2002 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and remitted to the IAT because the adjudicator erred in law by failing to give reasons on the torture issue.
enrichment.ratio: Where objective evidence of torture in the country of return is potentially relevant to the risk on return, an adjudicator must address it in reasons; failure to do so is an error of law even if the appellant's case was primarily directed at Syrian authorities.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in treating the 1998 incident as a criminal enterprise
Whether failure to address torture evidence amounted to an error of law
Whether the appellant's case was limited to fear of Syrian rather than Lebanese authorities
Whether new evidence not before the adjudicator could be relied on in the Court of Appeal

confidence.notes: Ground of appeal and remittal order are clearly stated; outcome on remitted appeal expressly not determined.

notes: Marriage ILR deception challenge; Elias J applied Khawaja and found deception proved to the higher civil standard.

enrichment.short_title: Kelly: judicial review dismissed where ILR obtained by sham marriage deception
key_facts: Jamaican claimant entered as a visitor, married a British citizen and obtained one-year leave, then indefinite leave to remain in March 2001.
The Home Office later learned the marriage was not subsisting at the time of the ILR application and interviewed the claimant under caution.
The wife's letter and police interview indicated the relationship had ended before the application; solicitors' instructions referred to cohabitation until 1999.
The Secretary of State contended ILR was obtained by deception under section 10 and issued removal directions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of removal directions following a finding that indefinite leave was obtained by deception.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the court was satisfied to the high civil standard that deception was used when ILR was applied for on 1 March 2001.
enrichment.ratio: On an allegation of deception in obtaining leave, the Secretary of State bears the burden of proof to a high degree of probability following Khawaja; inconsistent accounts and contemporaneous solicitor instructions may justify a finding of deliberate deception as to a subsisting marriage.
legal_issues: Whether the relevant date for assessing deception was the application date or decision date
The standard and burden of proof for section 10 deception
Whether the claimant's marriage was subsisting when ILR was applied for
Weight to be given to the wife's letter and deception interview answers
linked_authorities: Khawaja v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1984] 1 AC 74

confidence.notes: Detailed factual analysis and clear dismissal on deception.

notes: Supplementary confiscation time-to-pay judgment; pending appeal does not suspend payment periods.

enrichment.short_title: May: confiscation time-to-pay runs from Crown Court order despite appeal
key_facts: Following earlier confiscation appeals, May's order stood at £3,264,277; Stapleton's was reduced to £1,615,789; Bravard's to £626,383; and Fowles' to £40,000.
Appellants argued time to pay should run only after any appeal was finally determined and that reducing payment periods would increase penalty.
The court held payment periods had been running since the original Crown Court orders.
Further payment periods were fixed for Bravard and Fowles; certification for appeal to the House of Lords was refused on one point and conditionally offered on another.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further written submissions to the Court of Appeal on provisional time-to-pay periods after confiscation appeals.
enrichment.outcome: May's three-year period unchanged; Stapleton's period left expiring on 2 August 2005; Bravard ordered to pay within four months and Fowles within three months from 28 January 2005.
enrichment.ratio: An pending appeal does not suspend enforcement of a confiscation order or the running of time to pay; defendants should not assume success and may take preparatory steps to raise funds while appeals are pending.
legal_issues: Whether time to pay under a confiscation order runs from the Crown Court order or final appeal
Whether varying payment periods after a successful appeal amounts to a more severe penalty
Appropriate further periods where original time limits had expired
Whether to certify a point on joint benefit under section 71 of the 1988 Act
index_terms: Greater Manchester Probation Committee v Bent
linked_authorities: Greater Manchester Probation Committee v Bent [1996] 160 JP Rep 297

confidence.notes: Supplementary procedural judgment; principal confiscation reasoning was in the earlier January 2005 judgment.

notes: Landmark CPA challenge; automatic CSCI zero-star downgrade held unlawful fettering under section 99.

enrichment.short_title: Ealing v Audit Commission: CPA downgrade for zero CSCI star held unlawful

statutes_considered.title: Health and Social Care (Community Health and Standards) Act 2003

key_facts: Ealing scored 3 on core service performance and council ability under the 2004 CPA framework but received a zero CSCI social care star rating.
Rule 2 of the CPA framework capped overall categorisation at 'weak' where social services scored below one star.
Ealing challenged automatic downgrading without the Audit Commission applying its own mind to CSCI's reasons.
Walker J held section 99 required the Audit Commission itself to assess whether downgrading was warranted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent judicial review of the Audit Commission's 'weak' comprehensive performance assessment categorisation.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; automatic downgrading triggered solely by CSCI's zero star rating was unlawful and the categorisation approach was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 99 the Audit Commission must make its own findings and categorisation; it may adopt specialist inspectorate conclusions but cannot apply an automatic rule that refuses to consider representations where a rating may be determinative of downgrading.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 2 unlawfully fettered the Audit Commission's discretion
Whether CSCI star ratings were 'findings' or value judgments for section 99 purposes
Whether the Audit Commission abdicated its statutory function to CSCI
Whether Ealing could challenge the categorisation without challenging the CSCI rating itself
linked_authorities: Lavender & Sons v Minister of Housing and Local Government [1970] 1 WLR 1231
Parker v Camden London Borough Council [1986] 1 Ch 162

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of section 99 and clear quashing on the dictation ground.

notes: Transitional mandatory life tariff review; 16-year notified minimum term upheld for double honour killing.

enrichment.short_title: Haq: transitional mandatory life minimum term fixed at 16 years less remand
key_facts: Abdul Haq was convicted in 1991 of murdering his sister and her lover in an honour killing planned under family direction; bodies were dismembered and concealed.
The trial judge recommended 20 years and the Lord Chief Justice 15 years; the Home Secretary set a 16-year tariff.
Haq applied under Schedule 22 for High Court determination of the minimum term for an existing mandatory life prisoner.
The court could not set a term greater than the 16 years notified by the Secretary of State.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court determination under Schedule 22 of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 for a transitional mandatory life prisoner.
enrichment.outcome: Minimum term fixed at 16 years less 7 months and 7 days on remand, giving 15 years 4 months and 23 days; exceptional progress in prison did not justify reduction below the notified tariff.
enrichment.ratio: On a Schedule 22 review the court must assess seriousness by reference to Schedule 21 principles and judicial recommendations but cannot exceed the notified minimum term; post-sentence progress must be exceptional before it reduces the tariff for grave double murder.
legal_issues: Whether Schedule 21 starting points applied to transitional cases
The appropriate starting point for a 1991 double murder
Whether exceptional progress in prison justified reducing the tariff below 16 years
Whether the court could adopt the judicial recommendation rather than conduct its own assessment
linked_authorities: R (Anderson) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UKHL 46

confidence.notes: Full statutory analysis and explicit minimum term calculation.

notes: Patent claim construction appeal; upstream lyophilization did not infringe ready-to-use solution claim.

enrichment.short_title: Pharmacia v Mayne: no infringement where API was upstream lyophilizate
key_facts: Pharmacia sued for infringement of UK patent 2,178,311 covering injectable ready-to-use anthracycline glycoside solutions.
Mayne's epirubicin product used bulk lyophilized active ingredient dissolved and formulated into a ready-to-use solution.
Claim 1 required a solution 'which has not been reconstituted from a lyophilizate'.
The deputy judge held non-infringement; the Court of Appeal allowed Pharmacia's appeal on construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patentee's appeal from a streamlined declaration of non-infringement action under CPR Part 63.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Mayne's product did not infringe because upstream lyophilization of the API did not mean the final solution had been reconstituted from a lyophilizate.
enrichment.ratio: Purposive construction of a product claim focused on the final ready-to-use solution; the limitation excludes solutions made by reconstituting a lyophilized vial product, not solutions formulated from lyophilized raw material used upstream.
legal_issues: Whether 'not been reconstituted from a lyophilizate' excluded any upstream lyophilization
The relationship between product claim 1 and process claim 31
Application of Kirin-Amgen and Technip principles of claim construction
Where to draw the line between permissible formulation and excluded reconstitution
linked_authorities: Kirin-Amgen Inc v Hoechst Marion Roussel Ltd [2004] UKHL 46
Catnic Components Ltd v Hill & Smith Ltd [1982] RPC 183

confidence.notes: Single-issue construction appeal with detailed reasoning from Jacob LJ.

notes: EIA judicial review; planning permission quashed where ES left significant emission effects uncertain.

enrichment.short_title: Hereford Waste Watchers: planning permission quashed for inadequate EIA information

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Herefordshire Council granted permission for a 100,000-ton steam autoclave waste treatment facility at Madley using largely untested combined technology.
The environmental statement assumed negligible process emissions and deferred pollutant analysis to post-permission conditions.
The planning officer expressed reservations about negative pressure containment and lack of analysed steam samples.
Elias J quashed permission because significant environmental effects were not assessed before grant and consultation was frustrated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning permission for a waste recycling facility requiring environmental impact assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on the EIA ground; planning permission quashed, but the BPEO/floodplain challenge failed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a planning authority is uncertain whether process emissions may have significant environmental effects, it must obtain sufficient information in the environmental statement before granting permission; deferring material assessment to conditions undermines the EIA consultation scheme.
legal_issues: Whether the authority concluded there were no significant environmental effects from autoclave emissions
Whether conditions requiring pre-commencement pollutant reports were lawful under the EIA Regulations
When mitigating measures may be relied on without further ES information
Whether an alternative Rotherwas site was wrongly rejected on floodplain grounds
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Berkeley [2001] 2 AC 603
Smith v Secretary of State for the Environment [2003] EWHC 262
Bellway Urban Renewal Southern Ltd v Gillespie [2003] EWCA Civ 400

confidence.notes: Detailed EIA analysis and quashing; BPEO ground rejected separately.

notes: Professional negligence trial; solicitors not liable where key witness Evans was not called and understood CCA risk.

enrichment.short_title: Accident Assistance v Hammonds: solicitor negligence claim dismissed on credit-hire CCA risk
key_facts: Accident Assistance operated a credit-hire business acquired by GE; Dimond v Lovell later damaged recoverability of hire charges.
The claimant sued Hammonds Suddards Edge for failing to warn that standard agreements might be non-compliant with the Consumer Credit Act 1974.
Leading counsel Mr Hirst QC had advised on enforceability and recoverability risks; the firm's key client contact Mr Evans was not called by either side.
Hart J found Evans likely understood the advice and the solicitors were not liable for failing to re-emphasise it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a professional negligence claim against solicitors advising a credit-hire company before and after GE's acquisition.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the defendant firm was not liable because the claimant failed to prove Evans did not understand the implications of counsel's advice.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors are not negligent for failing to repeat advice already given by leading counsel where the court infers the client understood the risk; parties may deprive the court of decisive witness evidence by choosing not to call a key witness supportive of the defendant.
legal_issues: Whether the solicitors should have explained Consumer Credit Act non-compliance risks to Mr Evans
What inferences arise from neither party calling Mr Evans
Whether Evans understood Mr Hirst QC's advice on enforceability and recoverability
What Evans would have done if the risks had been further emphasised

confidence.notes: Long fact-heavy judgment; core dismissal reasoning on Evans' understanding is clear.

notes: Beneficial interest trial; claimant failed to prove half-share purchase agreement and cash contribution.

enrichment.short_title: Popely v Heltfield: half-share land trust claim dismissed for insufficient proof
key_facts: John Popely claimed a 50% beneficial interest in Bromley development land registered in Heltfield Properties Ltd.
He alleged an oral joint venture with his brother Ronald, £20,000 cash paid to the vendor, and purchase through nominee company Maltcrown.
The land later transferred to Heltfield; Popely's account changed materially during litigation and Ronald was not a party.
The judge found insufficient proof of the agreement and cash payment despite an IOU and an equivocal comfort letter from Stephen Blake.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of a claim for a resulting or constructive trust, share ownership and sale of registered land.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; caution to be vacated; Popely failed to establish a beneficial interest on the balance of probabilities.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant relying on unrecorded cash contributions and oral joint-venture agreements must prove them cogently; inconsistent accounts and uncorroborated cash-payment allegations will fail even where surrounding company dealings appear suspicious.
legal_issues: Whether Popely and Ronald agreed to buy the land in equal shares
Whether Popely paid £20,000 cash to the vendor on completion
Whether any trust interest bound Heltfield on a later transfer for stated consideration
Whether Popely had gifted his interest to his son Andrew
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank Plc v Rosset [1991] 1 AC 107
Lyus v Prowsa Developments Ltd [1982] 1 WLR 1044

confidence.notes: Extensive fact findings; dismissal on burden of proof is explicit though judge expressed residual uncertainty.

notes: Witness contempt appeal; finding quashed where appellant had no actual notice of witness summons.

enrichment.short_title: Wang: witness contempt quashed where summons not actually received
key_facts: Wang, a Mandarin-speaking witness in an immigration conspiracy trial, was warned by police on 6 May 2004 to attend court but no witness summons yet existed.
He left his required Aberystwyth address within 48 hours and was later arrested under a bench warrant.
A witness summons was posted through the letterbox on 24 May after he had gone; the judge found deliberate evasion and committed him for one month.
The Court of Appeal held contempt under section 3 required disobedience to a summons of which the witness had notice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal as of right against a Crown Court finding of contempt under section 3 of the 1965 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Finding of contempt quashed; mere failure to cooperate with the prosecution before a summons was issued and served was not enough.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 3 of the 1965 Act contempt requires disobedience without just excuse to a witness summons; where the witness had no actual notice of the summons, deliberate absence before it was issued cannot sustain a section 3 finding.
legal_issues: Whether police warning created an obligation enforceable as contempt before a witness summons issued
Whether posting a summons to an address the witness had unlawfully left amounted to sufficient notice
Whether common law contempt survived alongside section 3 where the witness evaded anticipated service
Application of R v Abbott to oral notification of summons requirements
linked_authorities: R v Robert Abbott [2004] EWCA Crim 91

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and quashing are clearly reasoned; common law contempt left open on alternative facts.
